record.title: An occupational audit finds LLM judges rank responses better than they match worker score levels
record.summary: The authors evaluate 33 LLM-judge configurations against 4,501 held-out worker ratings spanning 307 occupations in a US English text corpus. They report above-chance tie-aware response ranking for all configurations, while predicted acceptance shares range from 3.0% to 97.9% against the sampled workers’ 61.1%. A prespecified validation contrast within one fine-tuned lineage reports that a bundled few-shot/listwise protocol improves ordering while reducing task- and occupation-level agreement. The study audits agreement with sampled worker ratings; it does not measure objective work quality, AI productivity or employment effects.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or validation on multi-rated, employment-weighted occupational data.

brief.importance_rationale: If similar judge-scale mismatches occur in broader occupational measurement, estimates derived from AI task benchmarks could change materially. This study is an audit of one sampled US English rating corpus, not a measure of workplace productivity or employment effects.
limitations: Each response has one worker rating; sampled worker judgments are not noise-free ground truth.
Occupation-level split-half reliability is low; the source reports 0.093.
The US English text corpus is not employment-weighted; occupations and response-generator variants overlap across splits.
Most test comparisons were exploratory after repeated inspection; the prespecified protocol contrast bundles several changes.
No real workplace output, productivity, hiring or employment effect is measured.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report that ranking agreement can coexist with large mismatches in score levels and occupation aggregates.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary paper specifies the corpus, splits and judge configurations; the research desk did not independently reproduce its analysis.
technical.mechanism: Compares pointwise and listwise judge configurations with worker ratings at response-ranking, score-calibration, acceptance-share and occupation-aggregate levels.
technical.regime: 4,501 held-out ratings from 307 occupations in one US English text corpus; 33 existing judge configurations across six model families.
technical.strongest_baseline: Sampled worker ratings provide the study’s reference, with acknowledged low reliability at occupation level; they are not objective ground truth.

brief.title: An occupational audit finds LLM judges rank responses better than they match worker score levels
brief.why_it_matters: Occupational AI assessments can change when judge scores are converted into acceptance shares or occupation-level estimates. The paper shows that response ordering and score-level agreement are distinct measurement targets in one corpus, while leaving worker-reference reliability and transfer to real workplace outcomes unresolved.
